task.question: I hold 40% NVDA, 30% MSFT, 30% AAPL — should I add 15% TSLA?
task.name: TSLA

read_as.summary: add 15% TSLA to 40% NVDA / 30% MSFT / 30% AAPL

lines: At 15%, TSLA would carry 18% of the book's risk, inside the 25% budget; 19% is the most that stays inside.
The book's concentration is NVDA, not TSLA: after the trade NVDA carries 47% of the risk at 34% of the money. If that is the worry, trimming NVDA to 21% brings it inside the 25% budget.
Fill it as 60% near-touch limit then 40% market for $15,000, about 7.1 bps all in on the live book (one market order: 7.6 bps).

What would change the call: if TSLA outruns the rest of the book by 33%, it drifts past 19% of the book and back over the budget; trim it to 15% then. A jump in its correlation with the book lowers that ceiling, so re-ask after a large move.

steps.title: What the trade does to your book
steps.engine: your book's risk on 30 days of hourly returns
lines: Bottom line: to keep TSLA under 25% of book risk, size it at no more than 19% — the 15% proposed is inside that budget.
At 15% of the book, TSLA would carry 18% of your total risk.
Open-session beta 0.94 → 1.01
Risk spread across 2.5 → 3.2 effective position(s)
Most correlated with NVDA at +0.36; partly the same trade; the diversification is real but smaller than the position count suggests
Hedge: short QQQ worth about 101% of the book's value neutralises its market exposure (book beta 1.01); it does nothing for single-name news risk.
After the trade: NVDA 34% weight / 47% risk; AAPL 26% weight / 20% risk; TSLA 15% weight / 18% risk; MSFT 26% weight / 16% risk.
In the book's worst 5% of hours (an average loss of 0.40% an hour), TSLA would carry 16% of the loss, against 18% of the ordinary swing.
If QQQ falls 5%, the book moves about -5.0% through beta alone.
If QQQ falls 10%, the book moves about -10.1% through beta alone.
Realised worst case: the worst 24-bar window in the observed history would have moved this book -2.05% — driven by TSLA -7.83%, MSFT -1.94%, AAPL -1.81%
Sectors after the trade (Yahoo's classification, GICS names): Information Technology 100% → 85%, Consumer Discretionary 0% → 15%.

Factor loadings before → after (daily regression on SPY, IWM minus SPY, MTUM minus SPY, VLUE minus SPY, QUAL minus SPY, USMV minus SPY, IEF and BTC): market 1.08 → 1.15, size -0.22 → -0.16, momentum -0.20 → -0.17, value -0.28 → -0.28, quality -0.18 → -0.41, low vol -0.57 → -0.57, rates -0.28 → -0.27, crypto 0.01 → 0.03. Ask "what are my exposures" for the t-statistics.

How far to trust that beta: on 1,800 test books, it missed the next four weeks' realised beta by 0.24 on average. weekend-copilot, an S2 entry answering this same question, missed by 0.55 as it ships (p = 0.01) and by 0.36 on the same benchmark (p = 0.10, not significant); simply assuming a beta of 1.0 missed by 0.30. The QQQ-fall lines were off by 0.92 points on the 39 days QQQ really fell 1% or more (skfolio's vine copula: 1.00), and they are a centre, not a worst case

steps.title: How to execute the size
lines: Bottom line: in one market order this costs about 7.6bps (6.0bps fee + 1.6bps book impact) — the book absorbs it, so splitting saves little beyond the passive fills.

A $15,000 order is 1.11% of TSLA's 24h volume ($1,349,536); the fees come to about 6.0bps, and the square-root impact law — calibrated on Bitget's own books, at TSLA's own 251bps daily volatility — puts this size's market impact near 9.1bps; the live book below shows what taking it at once costs.
Plan: the stock's own market is shut, so this book is thin and resting orders tend to fill only when the price moves against them — passive orders get less of the size, not more.
Order book (buy side, live): taking all $15,000 at once walks 8 level(s) for 1.6bps of slippage on top of the fee.
Slice 1: 60% ($9,000) as near-touch limit — about 6.0bps fee plus 1.1bps book impact.
Slice 2: 40% ($6,000) as market — about 6.0bps fee plus 1.1bps book impact.

Schedule (Almgren-Chriss optimum, inventory decaying e-fold over 3 hour(s)): trade 39%, 32%, 29% of $15,000 hour by hour — expected cost 8.1bps with a one-standard-deviation risk of ±23.1bps, against 8.1bps ± 25.5bps for an even split, with the slice styles above applied inside each hour. Impact is priced from sweeping one hour's share of the order on the live book.

Cadence: send each hour's share as one-minute children, as Bitget's own TWAP does at a 60-second interval. Replaying a full day of Bitget's NVDA order book, $5,000 orders cost 6.3bps with fees in one-minute children against 7.6bps in hourly ones (Bitget's TWAP: 6.3bps; all at once: 9.4bps).

Waiting costs too: at this volatility the price drifts an expected 4.4bps in the minute between deciding and the first order landing, 13.9bps in ten — a cost of deliberating, separate from the impact above.
